definition: Slow to believe a claim and wanting good reasons or proof before accepting it.
example: Many scientists stayed skeptical of the surprising result until other labs repeated the experiment.
nuance: Unlike cynical, which assumes people have selfish motives, skeptical means holding back belief in a claim until there is evidence.
prompt: A car dealer insists that a ten-year-old car has never needed a single repair.
options: The buyer was skeptical of the claim and asked to see the maintenance records.
Fully skeptical of the dealer, the buyer signed the contract without a single question.
The scrape on the mechanic's arm turned skeptical and needed antibiotics.
The buyer's son was so skeptical about the car that he cheered and hugged the dealer.
reasons: Asking for proof before accepting a hard-to-believe promise shows reasonable doubt.
Signing without asking anything shows complete trust, the reverse of doubt.
This confuses the word with septic, which describes infection, not doubt.
Cheering and hugging show delight and trust, not a reluctance to believe.

practice.prompt: A classmate shares an online post claiming that eating carrots lets people see in total darkness.
options: Maya was skeptical and looked for a reliable science source before sharing the post.
Being skeptical, Jordan immediately forwarded the post to everyone in his contacts.
The teacher called the claim skeptical because it was written in such a confident tone.
Priya was skeptical, so she began eating carrots at every meal to see better at night.
reasons: Checking the evidence before passing along a strange claim is exactly this kind of doubt.
Spreading a claim right away shows ready belief, not careful doubt.
A doubtful claim is dubious; the people who doubt it are the ones who are skeptical.
Changing her habits to follow the claim shows she believed it without question.
